sentences.text: Physornis is recognized as one of the largest known terror birds.

Because the fossil record is incomplete, estimating the full size of this animal is challenging, yet its mandible branches are positioned further apart from the median line than those of Phorusrhacos, indicating a broader skull base.
The lower jaw features a constricted symphysis that is wide and possesses a flat underside.
A single preserved lower jaw specimen measured exactly 15 cm in length.
Large expansions of the lacrimal bone above the eyes suggest the animal hunted by sight in open, sunlit areas rather than shaded forests.
The genus was scientifically described by Florentino Ameghino in 1895.

Fossils have only been found in Deseadan deposits within the Santa Cruz and Chubut Provinces, with the first specimens discovered in the Pyrotherium beds near Puerto Deseado in eastern Santa Cruz Province.
Later, an Amherst College expedition to Argentina's Sarmiento Formation began in 1911.
Physornis was flightless, a conclusion supported by the proportional size of its wings relative to its body mass, with wing size being more reduced in larger group members.
Sharing characteristics with graviportal, large-bodied dromornithids and Gastornis, Physornis was a graviportal ambush hunter rather than a runner like Phorusrhacos, Procariama, and Psilopterus.
This species held a graviportal macropedatory ecological role.
Physornis likely preyed on large mammals.

Dreyer and colleagues examined bone samples from the FM-P13619 limb bones using ground-section microscopy to study growth, revealing a pattern of rapid growth similar to modern birds indicated by a transition from vascularized to laminar bone tissue, with fossils lacking lines of arrested growth that would indicate pauses.
Researchers suggest that cursoriality and graviportality exist on a spectrum, and Physornis may have been capable of short, fast bursts of speed.
Argentine paleontologist Federico Agnolín established the subfamily Physornithinae for Physornis and Paraphysornis in 2007.
Alvarenga and Höfling classified Physornis as a close relative of Paraphysornis and Brontornis, noting Brontornis is now a galliform.
Brodkorb and other studies have considered Aucornis eurhynchus a synonym of P. fortis, a species name used in the context of Physornis taxonomy.
The species formerly known as P. brasiliensis is now classified in the genus Paraphysornis.
Fossils of this genus date from the Oligocene to the Miocene epochs.
The animal lived during the Oligocene epoch in what is now Argentina and South America.

In 1941, Bryan Patterson suggested the holotype might not be avian, speculating it could be a fragment from a giant mammal like Parastrapotherium or Pyrotherium, and he provisionally classified the holotype as a nomen dubium.
There is a discrepancy in the recorded time range for Physornis, with one source citing the Oligocene while the Paleobiology Database lists a range from the Rupelian to the Late Pleistocene.
